messages.mes:
The road took him down between plowed fields where a carter nodded once from his seat and nothing else about him earned a second look. Up close the walls of Glassmere were older than they'd seemed from the verge — moss in the mortar, a gatehouse with its door folded back against the stone, traffic of carts and geese and a woman carrying a bolt of grey cloth through the shadow of the arch.

The gate guards watched the road, not the travelers. One glanced at the staff slung across Alaric's back, took in the plain robes, and looked elsewhere. A Mage student, probably, was the reading of it, and worth no more attention than the geese.

Inside, morning noise closed over him: hammering from a side lane, bread smell drifting from a shuttered counter being opened by a baker's boy, water running in the gutter down the street's center. A chalkboard outside a chandler's shop listed tallow and wax prices in a hand nobody rushed to read. Somewhere a bell rang twice and stopped.

The Guild hall stood where a pointing thumb had indicated — two streets over, past a fountain with a chipped basin. A painted board hung above its door: crossed sword and staff beneath a blue shield, paint flaking at the shield's rim. Doors of dark oak stood open to the morning.

Inside was cooler, dimmer after the bright street. A long counter ran along the left wall, and behind it a woman with cropped iron-grey hair was counting coin into a leather tray, her lips moving with the sums. To the right, a corkboard thick with paper slips caught the light from the high windows. A few tables held early occupants — two men over maps and a mug, a hooded figure asleep with their boots up near a hearth that still held last night's ash.

The woman at the counter finished her count, looked up, and set the tray aside.

"Morning. Registering, or here about work?"

"Red." She said it back flatly, already reaching under the counter. "Fine. Guild registration runs two silver, one time, and it buys you the lot — the board, the brokered materials, the protection of the rolls when a contract goes sideways. You start at Novice, whatever you can do. That's a separate thing." She set a heavy ledger on the counter and opened it to a fresh page, the parchment ruled in faded red lines. "Power Rank we measure with a stone when you sign. It goes in the book, but the Guild doesn't grant it and can't take it away. It's yours."

A quill came out of a jar, its feather bent at the middle. She smoothed the ledger page with one hand.

"Name as you want it written. Age if you'll give it — most do, it saves arguments later. I'll need the two silver before the ink dries, not after." She looked up at him properly for the first time, gaze ticking once over the robes, the staff, then his face. "Glassmere gets a lot of academy students signing on for pocket money. Most quit by winter."

The tray of coin she'd been counting sat at her elbow, deliberately moved out of reach of the transaction. Behind him, one of the men over the maps laughed at something and went back to pointing.

"So. Two silver, and the quill's yours."

messages.mes:
The two silver crossed the counter and disappeared into the tray with the rest of her morning's coin. She dipped the bent quill, wrote Alaric Red into the ledger in a hand that sloped hard to the right, and said, "Age?"

Whatever he gave her went under his name in smaller letters. Then she reached below the counter again and brought up a flat crystal the size of a paving stone, set in a wooden frame worn dark by years of hands. She turned it so it faced him.

"Hand flat on the crystal. It reads what you are — that's all. Doesn't hurt."

The crystal was cool under his palm. A dim light stirred deep inside it, amber, then steadied. She read the glow, took up the quill, and wrote a single letter beside his name.

"F," she said. "Starting point. Most everyone starts there or close to it." The crystal went back under the counter. "Now the plate."

She laid it on the counter between them: a thin stamped plate of pale tin-grey metal, the Guild's crossed sword and staff pressed into it, his name struck beneath in plain capitals. NOVICE sat under the name in smaller type.

"Don't lose it. Replacement's another two silver, and no, there's no discount for honesty about how you lost it." She closed the ledger and pushed it aside. "That's you done. Novice takes Novice work and below off that board — the blue slips. Don't take a white slip, the desk won't let it go active for you anyway, and you'll look foolish asking."

She glanced past him at the corkboard, where paper slips hung in rows, some blue-edged, some white, a few yellowed at the corners from hanging too long.

"Blue slips are small work. Deliveries, culls, things the Guild guarantees. Something catches your eye, bring it here and I'll make it active. Payment posts when the client deposits, and it pays at this desk when you turn in the proof. Not before." She was already reaching for her coin tray again, the transaction closed.

messages.mes:
She took the slip from him and stamped it, the seal press thumping down with a sound like a door closing. "Active," she said, and slid it back across the counter — a blue-edged slip now bearing the Guild's mark in red wax.

He asked about the Grotto, and she looked up from the coin tray.

"Glimmerdeep. You'll want the north road out of Southgate, follow the stream — it runs out of the rock at the cleft, a morning's walk, maybe less if you push. Can't miss it. The stream comes out of the hillside and the cleft mouth is right there beside it." She leaned an elbow on the counter. "The academy holds the cleft — Vellior. They've a warden at the mouth, Emris Sall, gatekeeper for the site. He'll admit registered adventurers to the outer galleries. Tell him what you're about and he'll let you pass."

She tapped the counter with one finger, settling into the rhythm of a thing she'd said before.

"It's crystal caverns. Mana-fed crystal grows wild in there, glittering, pretty as you like. The beetles chew on it — that's your work. Outer galleries only; the deeper parts aren't in the contract and the academy doesn't want strangers wandering them. Crystal beetles and mineral slimes, mostly, in the outer reaches. Rank F, the whole site. Novice work, properly."

She straightened, and her tone flattened back to business.

"Now hear the shape of it. The client is Vellior Academy. Locals confirm the work is done — Sall will know when the swarms are down — but the Guild pays you. Sixty copper, at this desk, when you turn the slip in with the work confirmed. Nobody out there hands you coin. And it's a cull, so it stays a cull: kill enough beetles that the survey crews can walk their lines again, and Sall will say so."

She slid the coin tray aside and picked up her counting again.

"Questions about the site, ask Sall at the mouth. Anything else, ask now."

The clerk, hearing nothing more, went back to her coins.

Outside, Glassmere was awake: cartwheels on wet cobbles, a fish-hawker's cry, smoke standing straight off the chimneys in the still air. He asked a woman scrubbing her doorstep and she pointed him up the Leatherrow with her chin — "Thessaly's, the one with the blue lantern" — and went on scrubbing.

Thessaly's sat where a side street bent toward the market square, a narrow front with a blue glass lantern burning in the window even by day. Inside smelled of ink, dried herbs and something faintly burnt. Shelves ran floor to ceiling: jars of powdered reagent, bundles of chalk, rows of wands in a felt-lined case, ink in squat bottles, a rack of Skill Stones behind a mesh screen with prices written on paper tags. A bell over the door had announced him; from a back room came a man's voice, unhurried.

"Be with you directly."

The shopkeeper emerged wiping his hands on an apron — a heavyset man, spectacles pushed up into grey hair, and his eyes did a quick professional pass over Alaric's robes and starter staff, lingering on the staff the way a smith looks at soft iron.

"Mage, are you. Well, you've come to the right front." He nodded at the shelves as he came around the counter. "Chalk, ink, reagents, common scrolls, first-circle foci. Stones are behind the mesh — look, but I unhook them, that's the arrangement."

He leaned on the counter.

"What are you needing? And mind, I stock for working mages, not collectors. If it's cheap and useful you're after, say so and I'll not waste your morning."

messages.mes:
The road north out of Glassmere followed the stream, and the stream came from the hills, so the way was easy to find and easier to walk. Carts passed him early — quarry workers, a man driving pigs — and thinned as the ground rose. By mid-morning the city was behind him and the hills stood ahead, grey and green, with the stream running fast beside the road.

The cleft announced itself before he saw it: a break in the hillsides where the water poured out of the rock over a lip of stone, and beside it a path climbing to a tall narrow gap in the cliff. Someone had worked here a long time. The path was cobbled near the mouth, and iron stakes with lanterns hung on them lined the last stretch. The cleft mouth itself had been framed with dressed stone and closed by a gate of iron bars — new iron, well kept, with a small warden's hut built against the rock beside it and a woodsmoke thread rising from its chimney.

From the hut came the sound of someone splitting kindling. A moment later the axe stopped, and a man leaned out of the doorway — lean, sixty-odd, close-cropped white hair, an academy surveyor's badge on a cord around his neck. He looked Alaric over once, unhurried, from robes to staff.

"Well," the man said. "Robes and a Guild plate. You'll be here about the beetles, then, or you've lost your way badly."

He set the axe against the doorframe and came out, wiping his hands on his trousers.

"Emris Sall. Warden here for the academy." He nodded up the cleft. "Survey crews are sat back at camp till the swarms are dealt with, so any Novice walking up this path is beetle business. You're the first this week, mind."

messages.mes:
Emris leaned against the gatepost, glad enough of the pause from kindling.

"How it works. The academy holds the whole cleft, but we've only opened the outer galleries — that's the first chain of caverns past the gate, maybe half an hour's walking end to end, with side passages. Deep galleries are barred and warded, and I'll know if anyone goes past the markers, so don't. Your contract's the outer grottos and that's plenty."

He held up fingers as he went.

"How many can enter — no limit, it's not that kind of place. It's a cavern system, not a hole. On a working day there might be two survey crews and a few adventurers all in the outer reaches at once. This week it's dead quiet, so likely you'll have it to yourself. The gate stays open dawn to dusk while the contract's running; I close it at dusk and I don't reopen for shouting, so mind the light."

"Will others enter while you're in — could happen, could not. Adventurers don't check in with me, they just walk through. You'll hear them before you see them, most like. Beetles don't care who's whose, mind. A swarm coming off another party's fight will come at you just the same."

He pointed up the cleft, where the daylight fell into the first cavern mouth.

Outer galleries, you can still see daylight or lantern-glow from the mouth in most chambers. When the blue shine is all you've got, and the air goes still and warm, you're at the boundary. messages.mes:
"Gate's behind you at dusk," Emris called after him, and the iron bars sang softly as Alaric passed through.

The path climbed a short way between the cliff walls, cobbled and damp, and then the daylight opened into the first cavern and the whole character of the place changed at once.

Crystal grew everywhere. It ran in thick veins down the walls and burst from the floor in clustered spires taller than a man, every facet catching the grey light from the mouth and throwing it back faintly blue. Underfoot the cobbles gave way to smooth crystal-sheathed rock, and the stream's sound softened behind him as he went deeper, replaced by a quiet that had weight to it. The air was cool at first, tasting of wet stone, and the first chambers still showed daylight pale behind him when he looked back.

Side passages branched off — two of them in the first large chamber, dark mouths between the spires — and the main passage went on, bending left into deeper blue. The crystal grew denser with every step, exactly as Emris had said. Small heaps stood here and there near the walls: surveyors' gear, a crate, a coil of rope, left where the crews had abandoned them.

On the floor of the second chamber he found the first sign of what he had come for. Narrow grooves were scored into the crystal, shallow parallel scratches, and beside them a scatter of what looked like tiny glass chips. Something had been chewing here, and not long ago — one of the chips still rocked when his boot came near it.

The chamber was quiet. Blue light thickened ahead, where the passage went on.

messages.mes:
The word left his mouth and the parchment answered.

The scroll ignited the instant it left his fingers — not burning, but unravelling, the wax seal flashing white and the whole sheet coming apart into a ribbon of orange fire that unfurled in midair as it sailed over the nearest beetle's notched shell. It burst above the half-circle like a struck flint, and a wave of flame slapped outward across the vein, roaring, light blazing off every crystal in the chamber so that the whole grotto went orange for a breath.

Heat rolled back over Alaric's face and forearms, dry and sudden, tasting of scorched mineral. The beetles' clicking rose to a shrill chittering drowned under the fire's roar, shells flashing as the flames broke over them, and the stripped vein behind them caught with a thin blue flicker of burning residue. Smoke boiled toward the ceiling in a fat grey column.

When the fire guttered out — fast, hungry, over almost as soon as it had begun — the chamber reeked of char and hot stone. Shapes moved through the smoke along the vein, stumbling, some still carrying small flames clinging to their shells.

The scroll was ash before it reached the floor.
